articles.title: It’s Election Time Again
articles.author: W. D. Ehrhart
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. So here we are just days before the midterm election, and the anticipation is almost palpable. Last weekend, my wife and I went to a No Thrones No Crowns No Kings rally in our neighborhood, and the prevailing sentiment was clearly that a Big Blue Wave is about to sweep the Democrats into control of both the House and the Senate as well as making huge gains at the state level. I can’t help remembering that the prevailing sentiment in 2016 among Democratic voters and the political pundits was that Hillary Clinton was a shoo-in. How could she lose to a clownish buffoon who bragged about grabbing women by their genitals and claimed he could shoot someone on 5 th Avenue in broad daylight without consequences? But Democratic voters and the political pundits didn’t reckon on the ignorance, irrationality, venality, and bigotry of huge numbers of American voters. I’ve been told by at least one newspaper editor that I can’t say that; I’m not supposed to disparage my fellow citizens because I might insult them. All I can say to that is: so what? What are they gonna do? Vote for Trumpsters just to spite me? A significant portion of Americans don’t need me to encourage them to vote against their own self-interests, however backhanded my “encouragement” may be. Multiple elections since 2016 have demonstrated time and again that the MAGAMobster’s supporters don’t care about broken treaties or counterproductive tariffs, cuddling up to dictators or murdering civilians on the high seas, kidnapping foreign heads of state or waging unprovoked wars of choice, wrecking the White House while installing a gladiatorial arena on the lawn, ruining the Reflecting Pool while destroying the Kennedy Center, trashing our national parks and re-writing American history itself, gutting the environment or packing the Supremely Unjust Court with right-wing activist ideologues, surrounding himself with incompetent lackeys while engaging in blatant criminal corruption to the benefit of himself, his family, and his uber-rich friends. Related: All the News That’s Fit to Print? Whatever disillusionment may be developing among the MAGA ranks, as nearly as I can tell, seems to be based on the cost of gasoline and the price of eggs, not on the outrageously lunatic behavior of the grotesque parody of a president currently occupying what has become the Whitewash House. And that disillusionment is not likely to result in large numbers of MAGAMinions going out and voting for candidates like James Talarico, Sherrod Brown, Amy Klobuchar, or Abdul El-Sayed. After all, Trumpasaurus is not even on the ballot. And given MAGAVoters’ inability to understand that they’ve been getting screwed left and right not just by the current administration, but by the cowards in Congress who refuse to do their sworn duty to uphold and defend the Constitution, I have serious doubts about the outcome of the election that is about to take place. I have spent a lot of time in the past ten years trying to understand how so many people could be so thoroughly hoodwinked by this grifter and con artist, incapable of seeing what he really is or grasping the damage he is doing to their lives and the country we live in. And I think I have finally figured it out. The core of his support comes from white men. Yes, there are women who support Trump. The Daily Show’s Jordan Klepper repeatedly braved Trump rallies to interview, among the myriad white men, white women and even a few people of color. But it is white men who constitute the backbone of his support. And these men are convinced that, ever since the 1960s, women, people of color, homosexuals, and immigrants have stolen white men’s patrimony, white men’s right to privilege and domination, which they do not see as privilege and domination, but simply as what should be theirs by right. Related: Trying to Avoid Giving Up And these men are angry, furious, outraged. They believe all their problems and frustrations and disappointments and failures can be laid at the feet of these non-male, non-hetero, non-white upstarts. For the most part, they cannot say out loud what they think and feel and believe because it might have serious repercussions on their jobs and families and social relationships. But their president expresses the intolerance and bigotry and racism and hatred they feel, and he gets away with it. He glories in it. He basks in it. He speaks for them. He says what they cannot say. It doesn’t matter what he actually does. It doesn’t matter what his policies are or how they impact his supporters or what kind of damage they are doing to the nation and the world. Thoughtful people assume that voters are thoughtful people, but election after election in my lifetime, and long before my lifetime, has demonstrated that huge numbers of voters are not thoughtful or rational or capable of grasping the consequences of their vote. To say all this out loud is a kind of heresy, but history has proven me right time and time again. Related: The Sexual Picadilloes of Politicians So I just don’t have a whole lot of confidence that the voting public is going to behave any differently than it always has, and a lot of that voting public is going to act against its own self-interest and vote for candidates who either agree with their Felon-in-Chief or lack the courage to stand up to him. I hope I’m wrong. I hope all those folks who think a Big Blue Wave is coming turn out to be right. How could any sane person not hope for that result? But after a lifetime of disappointments—I am 78 years old—I find it all-but-impossible to place any faith in the majority of the American voting public doing the right thing on election day.

articles.title: Girl Child
articles.author: Elahe Amani
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. October 11, the International Day of the Girl Child, arrived amid a period of unprecedented turmoil and shifting political realities. From war and violence in Iran and Yemen to political unrest and violent protests across parts of Europe, including Albania and France, a climate of instability continues to threaten human rights, peace, and security. Across many parts of the world, the rise of religious extremism, authoritarian governance, and right-wing populist movements has intensified resistance to gender equality and undermined efforts to protect the rights, dignity, and safety of girls. Invoking tradition, religious authority, parental rights, and the preservation of the “natural family,” some of these movements seek to restrict women’s autonomy and weaken the institutions designed to protect women and girls. The recognition of the “girl child” as a distinct focus of international advocacy marked an important milestone in the global struggle for gender equality. At the Fourth World Conference on Women in Beijing in 1995, The Girl Child was established as one of the 12 critical areas of concern in the Beijing Platform for Action. This recognition affirmed an essential principle: discrimination against women often begins in childhood, and addressing gender inequality requires specific attention to the rights, needs, and experiences of girls. The Beijing Platform addressed discrimination in education, health and nutrition, child labor, violence, harmful practices, and girls’ participation in social, economic, and political life. It helped institutionalize the girl child as a central category in international women’s rights advocacy, connecting the inequalities girls experience in childhood with the broader structures of gender discrimination that shape their lives. In subsequent years, UN General Assembly resolutions continued to address the rights of the girl child, while international agencies expanded their focus on girls’ education, child marriage, violence, exploitation, and adolescent health. In 2011, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 66/170, designating October 11 as the International Day of the Girl Child. The annual observance created an international platform to advance girls’ rights, amplify their voices, and recognize their leadership. Related: Iran’s Employment Crisis Is Driving Women Out of the Workforce The terminology itself also deserves reflection. The term “girl child” served an important political purpose: it made girls visible in policy discussions where the broader categories of “women” and “children” could obscure their distinct experiences of discrimination. Yet the history of this terminology is not without criticism. Historian Sarah Bellows-Blakely, in her work on the history of girl-focused development, examines how international development institutions have sometimes portrayed girls in the Global South primarily as vulnerable victims in need of intervention, rather than as individuals with agency, political voices, and diverse lived experiences. This critical perspective invites us to ask an important question: Who defines girls’ needs, whose knowledge shapes international policy, and how can girls themselves become active participants in decisions affecting their lives? Why does the girl child deserve our urgent attention today? Because recognition alone is not enough. The rights of girls remain threatened by the intersecting realities of poverty, armed conflict, forced displacement, disability, discrimination, and humanitarian crises. For girls living at the intersection of these vulnerabilities, the consequences can be especially severe. Consider the scale of the challenges facing children worldwide. More than 520 million children, over one in five globally, live within 50 kilometers of violent conflict events, according to research published by the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO). Approximately 1.6 billion children live in countries affected by conflict. These figures reflect different levels of exposure: proximity to violent events does not mean that every child experiences violence directly, but it highlights the enormous number of children growing up amid insecurity and instability. In conflict-affected communities, the destruction of schools ( the air strike on Feb 28, 2026 on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab 120 children killed ), loss of livelihoods, displacement, and breakdown of protective institutions can further heighten these risks. Discriminatory laws, harmful practices, and inadequate enforcement of children’s rights may allow these conditions to persist. Girls who are already marginalized because of poverty, ethnicity, disability, displacement, or other forms of discrimination may face multiple and overlapping barriers to protection. Related: Mother’s Day 2026: Reclaiming Motherhood as a Call for Peace, Justice, and Collective Care Poverty presents another profound challenge. According to UNICEF, approximately 412 million children lived in extreme monetary poverty in 2024, while an estimated 417 million children in low- and middle-income countries experienced severe deprivation in at least two essential areas of life, including education, health, nutrition, housing, sanitation, and water. These figures include both girls and boys and illustrate the magnitude of childhood deprivation, while underscoring the need for more comprehensive, gender-disaggregated data. Poverty, conflict, displacement, and discrimination do not operate in isolation. They intersect and reinforce one another, creating conditions that place girls at heightened risk of exploitation, violence, and child marriage. When families face economic hardship, armed conflict, or displacement, girls may be forced to leave school, lose access to health care and other essential services, or face decisions that prioritize immediate survival over their rights, well-being, and future. In some circumstances, child marriage is used as a misguided coping mechanism to reduce a family’s perceived financial burden, respond to insecurity, or conform to entrenched social and cultural expectations. The consequences of child marriage can extend throughout a girl’s life: interrupted education, early pregnancy, serious health risks, exposure to domestic and sexual violence, diminished economic opportunities, and restricted participation in decisions affecting her own future. The loss is not only individual. Families, communities, and societies are also deprived of girls’ talents, knowledge, creativity, and leadership. Child marriage, therefore, must not be understood simply as an isolated cultural practice or an individual family decision. It must also be examined within the broader social, economic, political, and institutional structures that constrain girls’ choices, perpetuate gender inequality, and undermine their fundamental rights. Globally, the legal landscape remains deeply concerning. According to UNESCO’s HerAtlas data, only 26% of countries set 18 as the minimum legal age of marriage without exceptions. In approximately 54% of countries, exceptions permit marriage before the age of 18, while in 18% of countries, laws still allow marriage below 18. These figures illustrate the gap between recognizing 18 as the appropriate minimum age and establishing an absolute legal prohibition on child marriage. The WORLD Policy Analysis Center’s legal database identifies numerous countries and jurisdictions where laws may permit girls to marry before the age of 18 under certain circumstances. These include Bahrain, Djibouti, the Federated States of Micronesia, Iran, Kuwait, Lebanon, Mali, Mauritania, North Korea, Pakistan, Qatar, Sudan, Timor-Leste, and Yemen. The United Kingdom also requires a jurisdiction-specific distinction: Scotland and Northern Ireland permit marriage at 16 under applicable legal conditions. The database additionally identifies Bangladesh, Botswana, Brunei, and the United Arab Emirates as having religious or customary law exceptions that may permit marriage below 18. These classifications should be checked against current national and subnational legislation, as laws and exceptions change over time. Particularly alarming is the evidence emerging from Iran, where technology is being used in ways that may facilitate and normalize child marriage. The Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) published an investigative report titled Child Marriage in the Digital Age , examining the Iranian government licensed matchmaking platform Adam va Hava (“Adam and Eve”) and its role in facilitating the marriage of minors. According to HRANA’s investigation, although the platform’s terms reportedly state that female users must be older than 15, its registration system accepts birth years corresponding to children as young as 12. Search filters reportedly allow users to browse prospective spouses from age 13, making profiles of minors accessible. These findings raise serious concerns about the protection of children online and the normalization of marriage involving girls who have not reached adulthood. The investigation also examines the platform’s institutional connections. HRANA traces its ownership to the Imam Reza Society, led by Hossein Yekta, a senior figure associated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Yekta has been subject to European Union sanctions related to human rights violations. The platform has also reportedly received promotion through Iranian state media. HRANA situates its operation within a broader government-backed matchmaking system that expanded following the 2021 Youth Population Law, which encouraged the development of authorized matchmaking platforms. These developments must be considered alongside Iran’s Civil Code, which generally sets the minimum marriage age at 13 lunar years for girls and 15 lunar years for boys, while allowing marriage below those ages with the consent of a legal guardian and judicial approval. This framework falls far short of establishing 18 as an absolute minimum age for marriage and raises serious concerns about Iran’s compliance with international child-protection standards, including the principles of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The response from international civil society has been significant. HRANA and 23 other human rights organizations issued a joint appeal urging major technology companies to take action. They called on Google and Meta to remove the application from the Google Play Store and on Meta to address promotional accounts on Instagram and Threads. According to the appeal, an Instagram account with approximately 192,000 followers had been used to promote the platform and its matchmaking services, including content involving minors. The organizations also called for greater transparency regarding ownership, safeguarding measures, and the enforcement of child-protection policies. Related: Disconnected in War While after the joint appeal of HRANA and 23 other human rights organizations Google removed the "Adam and Eve" app from Google Play on October 9, 2026, for policy violations and Meta investigated the findings and removed related promotional and external entities from its platforms (including Instagram and Threads). However, this case raises a fundamental question: What responsibility do governments, technology companies, and international institutions have when digital platforms facilitate practices that place children’s rights and safety at risk? Technology should expand opportunities, access to information, and human connection, not provide new mechanisms for exposing children to exploitation or normalizing practices that compromise their autonomy and well-being. Child marriage is not simply a matter of tradition or private choice. When discriminatory laws permit it, institutions facilitate it, and digital platforms make it more visible and accessible, the issue becomes one of public accountability and the protection of fundamental human rights. Every girl has the right to childhood, education, bodily autonomy, safety, and the opportunity to determine her own future. Ensuring those rights requires unequivocal legal protections, effective enforcement, responsible technology governance, and sustained international action to eliminate marriage before the age of 18, without exceptions. The reality is that child marriage risks to girls' safety, physical integrity, health, and autonomy. In an extensive research on Child marriage and intimate partner violence: A global meta-analysis with the title of “ Prevalence of intimate partner violence among child marriage victims and the comparison with adult marriages: a systematic review and meta-analysis” 38 studies involving approximately 395,000 women married as children across five continents were reviewed and the findings are “ it is estimated that 35% had experienced intimate partner violence during their lifetime and 24% in the previous 12 months. Compared with women who married as adults, women married as children had 42% higher odds of experiencing intimate partner violence over their lifetime and 37% higher odds in the preceding year. Other research such as Honor-based violence against children: A systematic review with the title of “ Honor, violence, and children: A systematic scoping review of global evidence (2024) in the Journal Child Abuse & Neglect. This research identifies recurring harms including violence, family rejection and control, homicide, and forced or early marriage. The research highlights the risks of family violence and homicide, though it does not establish that child marriage itself causes honor killings. Child marriage in Iran and other countries where it is legally permitted requires a holistic examination of power dynamics, gender-based norms, and the ways violence is portrayed in the media and normalized in the public consciousness. The issue is not merely the occurrence of a crime, but also how such acts are represented sometimes in ways that normalize or even legitimize them. A crucial question is whether Iranian media is challenging these deeply rooted gender norms and defending women’s and girls’ fundamental rights to life, safety, and autonomy or, instead, reinforcing the very structures that undermine them. Combating so-called honor killings of the girl childs cannot be achieved simply by condemning perpetrators after the fact. It requires confronting the gender-based power structures that place girls in vulnerable situations, questioning the social and cultural norms that enable such violence, and ensuring that legal and institutional protections prevent child marriage and safeguard girls from harm. The legislative history of Iran’s Protection of Women Against Violence bill reflects the challenges of securing meaningful legal protection. Also referred to as the Protection, Dignity, and Security of Women Against Violence and later renamed the Prevention of Harassment and Promotion of Security for Women Against Misbehavior , the bill was reportedly withdrawn from the Islamic Consultative Assembly (Parliament) by President Masoud Pezeshkian’s cabinet in September 2025. For more than 15 years, the proposed legislation has moved back and forth among successive administrations, the judiciary, and Parliament, illustrating the prolonged struggle to establish comprehensive legal protections against violence toward women and girls. Related: March 8 in the Shadow of War: Iranian Women and the Enduring Struggle for Gender Justice Needless to say that child marriage is not only happening in global south. In the United States, as of October 8, 2026, 32 states reportedly still permit marriage before the age of 18 under certain legal conditions, including parental consent, court approval, or other exceptions. The laws vary significantly from state to state. California has recently prohibited marriage for anyone under 18, without exceptions, joining the states that have eliminated child marriage through legislation. The 32 states identified as still allowing marriage before age 18 are Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming. Nearly 300,000 children were married in the U.S. between 2000 and 2018. The vast majority were girls wed to adult men. Ending child marriage requires more than prohibiting marriage before the age of 18. It demands enforceable legal protections without exceptions, equal access to quality education, economic and social support for families, protection during humanitarian emergencies, and the meaningful participation of girls in decisions affecting their lives. On protecting the child girl rights, dignity and safety, we must move beyond celebrating girls’ potential and acknowledging their vulnerability. We must confront the structures that deny them safety, dignity, equality, and opportunity. Protecting girls means addressing not only the violations they experience, but also the intersecting inequalities and structural conditions that allow those violations to persist. Every girl deserves the freedom to grow up safely, complete her education, exercise autonomy over her life, and shape her own future. The promise of Beijing remains unfinished. Our responsibility is to turn its commitments into lived realities for every girl, especially those whose voices are too often unheard and whose rights are most at risk. Beijing Platform for Action, Section L: The Girl Child — United Nations ⁠ International Day of the Girl Child — United Nations ⁠ Child poverty and deprivation — UNICEF, more than 400 million children globally live in poverty ⁠ Children living near violent conflict — Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO) ⁠ Historical and critical analysis of the “girl child” terminology — Sarah Bellows-Blakely, scholarly article ⁠

articles.title: American Empire Is Running Out of Money
articles.author: Jack Rasmus
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. There is increasing public discussion today, in the US and globally, about the trajectory of the American Empire. The discussion frequently cites the American Empire’s increasingly apparent unwinnable wars in Iran and Ukraine; the Empire’s failure to check the rise of China economically, politically and technologically; the challenge to American global economic hegemony by the BRICS; growing splits in the NATO alliance between Europe and the US; the fracturing of long term economic and political relations with historically closest ally Canada; and the Empire’s resort to aggressive military and economic action within the western hemisphere—to name but the more obvious. A large part of the commentary pointing to these and other developments argues, correctly, they are signs of America’s imperial decline. Some extrapolate and hyperbolically argue—incorrectly—that the developments are signs of Empire collapse. But ‘signs’ aren’t necessarily causal explanations of decline and certainly not of collapse. More often the ‘signs’ are symptoms of more fundamental, underlying causal forces responsible for the increasingly obvious trajectory of American imperial decline—while extrapolations concluding collapse are impressionistic and distorted by wishful thinking. Empires do not decline because they lose wars, are abandoned by allies and client states, or are increasingly opposed by state challengers to their hegemony. Empires decline because they can no longer afford the expanding costs of maintaining their hegemony: the accelerating costs of waging constant wars of expansion and/or containment, the demands of financing a bloated expanding military bureaucracy, the inability to afford or develop new generations of weaponry, the necessity of supporting weakened and increasingly economically dependent allies, the costs of bribing foreign elites to continue to accept Empire leadership and rules, and the inability to maintain dominance over global goods and money asset flows. Empires are expensive to maintain and defend. That’s been true historically. It’s no less true of the American Empire today. Related: Fed Rates, US Treasury Market & Crisis of Empire The costs of the American Empire have been rising steadily since 2001. They accelerated after 2021, intensified further 2025-26 under the Trump regime. And promise to grow even faster the next two fiscal years, 2027-28. But accelerating costs is only half of the problem of imperial finance. Empire costs can rise and even accelerate so long as revenues continue to rise sufficiently to fund Empire institutions, its military and geopolitical practices. When revenues no longer rise proportionately to the rising costs—a Funding Gap necessarily arises. Insufficient revenue generation required in order to pay for the accelerating costs of Empire together create the Funding Gap. And the American Empire today is experiencing a sharply expanding Funding Gap, as its costs accelerate faster than its ability to generate sufficient revenue to cover the accelerating costs. In the 1990s decade there was no Funding gap. Rising expenses of Empire were financed by nearly 4% annual GDP growth and tax revenues from that growth. The transformation to a professional army, and the consequent reduction of 500,000 troops, also released significant cost savings. There was no resort to debt financing. In the latter three years of the decade the US actually ran a budget surplus. The decade represented the era of high ‘unipolarity’ of the American Empire. The situation began to change after 2000. Costs of Empire accelerated as US neocons launched ‘forever wars’. Economic growth annually slowed by nearly half. Simultaneously, American imperial elites embarked on a massive tax cutting experiment that would eventually delete $20 trillion from the US Treasury over the next quarter century. A Funding Gap began to emerge, relatively slowly at first. And the Empire began resorting to debt financing of that gap. The cost acceleration slowed in the first half of the second decade of the 21st century, as government finances in general were diverted to the economic bailout in the wake of the great recession and banking crash of 2008-09. By the end of that decade, however, Empire costs began to rise more rapidly once again. Economic growth recovered slowly and weakly, as did revenues from taxation which were further impacted negatively by Trump’s 2017 $4 trillion tax cuts. Then came the Covid crash of 2020-21 and further bailouts even more costly than 2008-09. Overlaid on this was a renewed acceleration in Empire costs at the fastest rate yet, as wars in the Middle East, Ukraine, and military buildup for planned war in Taiwan accelerated defense spending once again. The spending on war and defense accelerated further in 2025-26 as Trump launched no fewer than eight imperial offensives in 2025. The cost side of Empire promises to accelerate still further as Trump proposed to add hundreds of billions of dollars more to Pentagon and defense spending in 2027-28.While the costs of Empire continued to accelerate out of control, the revenue side of Empire began experiencing severe problems as well. Revenues to fund imperial activity may come from tax revenues from robust general economic growth. Or from debt sources as the Empire resorts to borrowing to cover its costs. Or some combination of revenues from both taxation and borrowing. But as costs of Empire have accelerated in the 21st century, tax sources have struggled to fill the emerging cost acceleration. Despite a $10 trillion fiscal-monetary stimulus in 2020-22, economic growth only modestly rose above 2% annually after 2021. A Trump second $5 trillion tax cut mostly on capital incomes in 2025 exacerbated the pressure on tax revenues as a funding source. The consequence was an even greater resort to debt financing of the rising costs and Funding Gap. Annual budget deficits exceeded $2 trillion on average after 2021, driving the national debt from $29.6 trillion in 2021 to more than $40.1 trillion in 2026. That’s an average of more than $2 trillion rise in national debt per year. The rise in deficits and debt in turn resulted in interest payments on the debt escalating from $562 billion in 2021 to $1.36 trillion in 2026. In other words, debt financing of the accelerating costs of Empire is fast approaching its limits—just as tepid economic growth and continued massive tax cutting further reduces tax revenues as a source of funding. Debt financing occurs primarily via the federal US government sale of US Treasury securities annually to foreign and domestic US buyers. The former constitute 32% of total Treasury holdings; the latter the remaining 68%. As costs of Empire accelerated rapidly in the past five years, debt financing was able to continue to fund the slack and cover the chronic multi-trillion annual deficits and national debt. However, events in 2026 indicate debt financing through Treasury sales may have entered a crisis period as well. Treasuries sales managed to continue to rise after 2021 as costs of Empire accelerated—even as China and other foreign buyers of US Treasuries reduced their purchases. China alone reduced its holdings of Treasuries from $1.2 trillion by half to $.6 trillion over the five year period. Related: The Coming AI Jobs Armageddon The empire’s closest ally, Japan, continued to purchase Treasuries, however, maintaining more than $1 trillion in total Treasury holdings. Meanwhile, Empire European allies accelerated their Treasury purchasing. Many EU countries (and Canada) doubled their purchases of Treasuries from 2021 to 2025. In short, the Empire’s closest ‘core’ allies largely funded the accelerating costs of Empire from 2021 through 2025. But this may be coming to an end in 2026, raising the specter the Empire can no long debt finance its runaway costs of Empire. In 2026 Japan began shifting from buying more US Treasuries to buying more of its own government bonds—as what is called the Yen ‘carrying trade’ collapsed and US Treasury Dept. intervention failed to restore the carrying trade. Simultaneously, the Empire’s European allies appear to have begun reducing their massive purchasing and holdings of US Treasuries—as their costs of funding their support for their Ukraine war required new bond issuance of $90 billion with a purported additional $177 billion in EU bond issuance to follow. In addition, Europe plans to fund a $1 trillion rise in European military production promises to add more to their bond debt load. With these developments, continued Europe (and Canada) buying of US Treasuries is highly unlikely—putting pressure on the Empire generating more Treasury sales from domestic US buyers. The Trump administration has tried to supplement Treasury sales with Tariff revenues. In 2024 total US revenue from tariffs was $88 billion. This initially rose to $288 billion in 2025 due to Trump’s initial tariff wars. But US Supreme Court decisions in 2026 required the return of $145 billion of that $288 billion. Trump tariff policies have therefore failed as a significant new revenue generating source to offset the slowing and possibly even decline of debt revenue from Treasury sales to foreign buyers. Foreign sales of Treasuries remain the primary source of funding of Empire costs, however. With purchases by China, Japan and Europe growing more uncertain, the Empire must sell even more Treasuries to domestic US buyers (banks, businesses, wealthy investors, etc.). But that source of debt financing too may be confronting a separate set of concurrent problems of its own. The bubble in the Artificial Intelligence financial markets has been ‘sucking up’ money capital in 2026 at an astounding rate. The big 7 tech companies alone project the need to raise $1 trillion in 2026 (and another $1 trillion in 2027) in order to fund investments in data centers, chips, AI agents, etc. The big Tech companies have largely committed their former mass of cash holdings and even resorted to raising equity (new stock) to generate additional revenues to invest in AI. Related: No Oil Shortage, Just War Profiteering They have also begun borrowing at a level as never before. Some estimates are that $200-$300 billion is being borrowed from private capital sources to fund the AI boom. If so, that amount will likely ‘crowd out’ and discourage further private US domestic purchases of US Treasuries in 2026-27. That development will further exacerbate the problem of debt financing of the Empire via Treasury sales, as costs of Empire continue to accelerate further under Trump, 2027-28.In other words, just as the costs of Empire accelerated after 2021, rose faster in 2025-26 and are projected to accelerate still faster in 2027-28, the ability of the Empire to finance its rising costs from traditional Treasury sales (foreign and domestic) is becoming increasingly problematic. The American Empire’s current Funding Gap is therefore likely to grow—as costs continue to accelerate and the primary (Treasury sales) and even secondary (tariff revenues) sources prove insufficient to keep up!In this writer’s just released new book, ‘ The Twilight of American Imperialism ’ , Clarity Press, September 2026, the data on costs of Empire and revenue sources—i.e. the Funding Gap of Empire—is provided in detail, with sources, for the period 1992 through 2026 (with projections beyond). The following Table 5.1 is from Chapter Five, ‘ The Crisis of Imperial Finance’ , of the book. It summarizes the accelerating total costs of Empire since 2019.Together, the trends in Empire costs vs. revenues reveal the American Empire’s Funding Gap is about to become unsustainable. The book further concludes, the Empire will subsequently have to cut costs by retreating to the western hemisphere and Central Pacific; or raise more revenue from taxation; or divert revenues from social programs to Empire expenditures. Or likely some combination of all the above. Like Empires before it—from the Roman to the British—it is the crisis in imperial finance which is ultimately driving the decline of the American Empire. The military failures, failed regime change operations, fracturing geopolitical alliances and geoeconomic developments are but symptoms and ‘signs’ of Empire decline. articles.title: Israel Fears NAZA. Why Don’t Our Films Scare Anyone?
articles.author: Alex McCarron
articles.content: It isn’t uncommon for states to retaliate against the filmmakers who insult them. Sergei Parajanov was imprisoned for daring to make poetic cinema in the era of Soviet Realism. Jafar Panahi’s twenty-year ban from filmmaking and six-year prison sentence have become the central theme of the very films the Iranian state seeks to suppress. Even in America, documentarians like Emile de Antonio, Errol Morris, and Frederick Wiseman have faced bans, bomb threats, and personal death threats. Within the long history of the repression of film and filmmakers, it’s hard to think of anything like the fury the Israeli state is raining down on the directors of NAZA , a new documentary tracing the IDF’s brutal campaign in Gaza. The reaction from the Israeli government has been unambiguously hostile. Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar has threatened to revoke the citizenship of directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. They’re also facing potential criminal prosecution from IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir and threats to their families by members of Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party, who’ve assembled outside Szor’s mother’s house chanting “Death penalty for traitors.” Netanyahu himself, no stranger to violent incitement against political opponents, compared the film to a barrage of ballistic missiles aimed at Israel. But these attacks have only served to elevate the profile of the film, which has been selling out theaters in New York and fueling the debate about who, if anyone, in Netanyahu’s coalition will end up in the Hague. As horrible as this ordeal must be for the filmmakers and their sources, one can’t help thinking that this reception speaks to the power art and journalism can have on national politics when it strikes the right nerve. American filmmakers should ask themselves why our films have lost this power to threaten the elite. Hasbara Gives Way to Brutal Repression Israel, to be sure, has its own special relationship to journalism and propaganda, which a film like NAZA was uniquely poised to disrupt. Hasbara, the Hebrew word for “propaganda,” was once an elegantly managed media ecosystem built on the grammatical obfuscations of New York Times and BBC headlines, on the one hand, and the self-serious “shoot and cry” films like Waltz with Bashir (2008) and Lebanon (2009), on the other. In these films, soldiers come close to reckoning with their war guilt, but only as personal trauma devoid of political context. Like most bad apologies, these stories seem like self-justification more and more as they progress: It was my first day on the job as tank gunner ; these terrorists keep using civilians as human shields ; mistakes were bound to happen . As Prime Minister Golda Meir once said, “We can forgive the Arabs for killing our sons, but we can never forgive them for forcing us to kill their children.” After a few post–October 7 news cycles, however, the hasbara began to crumble, and Israel launched a new stopgap: a campaign of international intimidation, blatantly corrupt media spin by powerful ideologues like Larry and David Ellison, and an unprecedented massacre of combat zone journalists. For Edward Said’s generation, the task of overcoming Israeli propaganda meant outspending and outmaneuvering an elegantly managed ideological apparatus. For the directors of NAZA , the challenge was simply finding the courage to tell the truth at a time when Western powers had given the green light to any and all forms of repression, reprisal, and bloodshed. For the time being, American film is still contained by its more or less subtle ideological apparatus, rather than outright skullduggery against filmmakers. Recently, the Warner-Paramount merger put a long list of media properties (CNN, HBO, TBS, BET, et al.) on the same path for political reeducation that CBS suffered under Ellison hatchet woman Bari Weiss. The move is a part of a longer historical assault on America’s ability to understand itself or the rest of the world. Corporate media conglomeration was already a corrosive force in American newsrooms, as were the economic pressures that came with the news avoidance of the Trump years, a result of his “flood the zone” approach to political theater and scandal. And that’s to say nothing of what social media has done to impoverish news outlets. A great effort is undertaken to keep Americans ignorant of certain truths — particularly when it comes to our history of military interventions. And once the job is done, it’s hard to see one’s own country clearly. Sometimes the only way to recognize our own propaganda is to watch how another country’s falls apart. How PTSD Is Used to Avoid Tougher Questions One glaring difference between the NAZA filmmakers and their counterparts in American media is that they took their subjects’ moral crisis seriously to begin with. It’s what gives the film its subversive power. When our veterans talk about their feelings of guilt for their participation in the global war on terror, our media treats it as symptoms of a psychological illness, one with a medical solution. A New York Times article from 2024 called “ A Secret War, Strange New Wounds ” is representative of the genre. The article spends most of its length illustrating the deteriorating lives of veterans suffering from hallucinatory PTSD, on the one hand, and inconclusive science about a new kind of head trauma, on the other. Questions like, What war were these soldiers fighting? In what region of the world were they located? What were they aiming their guns at exactly? are treated as unrelated asides. The soldiers profiled were a part of the US war on the Islamic State in Syria and Iraq. Because the political cost of boots on the ground was too high, the US elected for a strategy of overwhelming artillery bombardment at a volume and tempo not seen since Vietnam. The result was an unknown number of civilian casualties. The article begins with a haunting encounter between a veteran and the ghost of a little girl, covered in dust, who appears to him repeatedly in his home, following him from room to room, “[staring] at him with a glare as dark and heavy as oil.” The author states that the soldier thought the IS fighters he killed had put a hex on him, even though the figure haunting him wasn’t an enemy combatant. Yet it takes the author of the Times piece sixty-seven more paragraphs to ask what gunners like these were even aiming at. The answer: nothing in particular. The soldiers, from a top-secret special forces group known as Task Force 9, were firing into Raqqa in a grid pattern, indifferent to who or what they were hitting. Sometimes when they would elect to actually find targets, according to the Times ’ own reporting, they would deliberately select “mosques, schools, dams and power plants.” The group, it turns out, had been given “broad authority to use heavy firepower” by President Donald Trump. The article doesn’t spend any time exploring the psychological effect this kind of mass murder might have had on the soldiers or, for that matter, on the lives of the people on the other end of the shelling. America’s Own War Crimes Some Americans might say it’s unfair to compare our veterans to the IDF soldiers profiled in NAZA , but Israel’s conduct against Palestine isn’t that far from the atrocities we’ve visited on neighboring countries during the war on terror. The war in Iraq destabilized one of the most developed states in the region and killed as many as a million people, by some estimates. Throughout the war, the US did everything it could to exacerbate interfaith and tribal conflicts — the very tensions Saddam Hussein, deploying his own bloody methods, had successfully suppressed throughout his rule. This US strategy of tension included hiring notorious war criminal Colonel James Steele as a consultant to train the Shia militias who had infiltrated the interior ministry. Steele was one of the US handlers of the Salvadoran death squads deployed during their civil war, and he shared that experience with the Shia Wolf Brigade, which made a name for itself torturing and murdering Sunni civilians and insurgents alike with power drills. Our military even shared Israel’s enthusiasm for the outright leveling of cities. During the Second Battle of Fallujah, the US forces damaged or destroyed roughly 70 percent of the city’s buildings. And that’s just what we did in Iraq during the war on terror. One could go on about overt and covert antiterrorism operations reaching across the Middle East, all the way into Africa, and the extraordinary rendition and torture program that spanned the entire globe. The only person in global politics who seems interested in adjudicating America’s war crimes is Netanyahu himself, who routinely invokes Hiroshima and the Allied carpet-bombing of Japan and Germany whenever he receives calls for restraint from Joe Biden or Trump. As long as America fails to atone for its own historical guilt, nations like Israel will continue to claim our example as a legal precedent. A Soldier’s Guilt as a Disease to Be Cured It’s not just our politicians who have failed in this enormous task. The development of the American mind — our education, our culture, even our medical practices — evinces a trend toward mental and historical oblivion. In her recent book, Traumatized , Catherine Liu traces the history of the PTSD diagnosis as a well-intentioned project by antiwar veterans and psychiatrists to address the unique psychological dysfunction veterans experienced during the Vietnam War. Where they failed, the NAZA filmmakers succeeded. NAZA addresses war guilt head on in something like a public version of the talking cure, where exploring memories of war and complicity in war crimes is not only therapeutically valuable but politically volatile as well. The doctors who lobbied to include PTSD in the DSM, by contrast, treated guilt itself as a symptom of a mental disease. We often refer to mental disorders like depression and PTSD as “diseases” or “illnesses” even when there is no physiological trace. This use of medical terminology and symbolism was useful at the inception of psychoanalysis to get guilt-ridden Victorians to open up about oedipal fantasies, but as Liu points out, over time this relationship between therapy and the medical establishment resulted in drug companies displacing talk therapy in the search for cures and the development of the DSM from a statistical tool maintained for the US Census Bureau into a therapeutic tool whose use is required by insurance companies. The end result is that when veterans talk to us about their guilt, we talk to them about whether or not their helmets are doing a good job of protecting them from concussions. American war films have shared this myopic conception of the meaning of war, which is a shame, because many, like The Deer Hunter (1978) and Apocalypse Now (1979), are in fact great works of art made with extraordinary skill and ambition. It’s hard not to feel like some of the effort was wasted, though, when you measure the worth of these films against their own moral aims. Was the point to arrange artistic elements in a pleasing way? Or to stage a drama in a particularly conflict-prone environment? Or was it to change America’s attitude toward these pointless imperial adventures abroad? If it was the latter, even the best war films fail. François Truffaut famously stated you could never really make an antiwar film, because even the most horrific depiction of war feels exciting and heroic on screen — even some of its darker moments. There are plenty of anecdotal reports of soldiers amping themselves up for battle by watching the “This is my rifle, this is my gun” segment of Stanley Kubrick’s Full Metal Jacket (1987). The main problem with these films, though, is their narcissism. The filmmakers never make a serious attempt to understand what it’s like to be on the receiving end of American munitions. Pakistani British novelist Kamila Shamsie, in her wonderful essay “ The Storytellers of Empire ,” shows how rare this gesture is in American letters. She highlights the example of John Hersey’s Hiroshima as the exception that proves the rule. Hersey was the rare American author who actually went to visit the country we bombed before writing about it, and his book is built of six stories that grew out of interviews he did with survivors of the blast. Hiroshima is as concerned about how it would be read in Japan as it would be in America. War Films That Avoid the “Shoot and Cry” Problem The Palestinians, for their part, have not only always made great films but have made ones that make vital political gestures. Their filmmakers often employ styles that are popular in the international art house cinema of their time, sometimes to better effect than those they’re imitating. Leila and the Wolves (1984) is a great film about Palestinian and Lebanese feminism and struggle in the mode of one of those Agnes Varda or Jean-Luc Godard films that wander between documentary and lyrical vignettes. The Time That Remains (2009) uses the loud, ironic design of early-2000s Wes Anderson movies for comedy about an apartment that changes hands between an Arab and Jewish family during the Nakba. Neither film feels derivative of the styles they’re borrowing. The gesture the filmmakers are making is something like butting into a conversation at a party and gently steering the conversation toward what they really want to talk about. This not only has worth as a means of breaking through our heavily propagandized notions; it has a deeper moral purpose of returning cinema to the promise it once held as a means of international conversation, where the meaning of war isn’t personal, psychological guilt but a relationship between two peoples, both of whom deserve justice of one kind or another. When making a film as a political gesture, timing is also key. The “shoot and cry” films are often made years, sometimes decades, after the conflict has ended, when the dead are buried, the maps redrawn, and the spoils of war long since divided. There’s little the hand-wringing liberals can do to enforce retribution for the crimes of their state at that point. It’s important that NAZA directors Szor and Abraham are making this film now, when there’s still a chance the truth can affect an escalating situation. A thin hope, maybe, but a welcome one in this uniquely hopeless age.
